When you look at someone or something askance, you are looking at them with suspicion, distrust, or disapproval. You are not accepting them straightforwardly. Instead, you are eyeing them with doubt, caution, or quiet judgment.

Think of it this way: imagine a stranger offers you a piece of food from their bag on a bus. You don't outright refuse it, but you glance at it — and at them — with a quiet "something feels off about this" feeling. That guarded, doubting, wary look is the feeling that "askance" captures.

The word paints a small but vivid picture. Traditionally, looking askance meant looking sideways at something — glancing at it from the corner of your eye, slightly turning away, rather than looking at it directly and openly. This physical image feeds the emotional meaning perfectly: when you don't fully trust something, you don't face it head-on. You look at it sideways — cautiously, half-turned, not fully open to it.

Today, the emotional meaning is the dominant one. You don't have to literally move your eyes sideways. "Askance" simply means you are regarding someone or something with suspicion or disapproval.

"Askance" almost always appears with the verb "look." The standard construction is:

"to look askance at" someone or something

You will almost never see "askance" used outside this kind of construction. It is a word that is deeply married to the act of looking — whether literally or figuratively.

Here are clear examples that show the word in action. Notice how each one carries a flavour of doubt, wariness, or disapproval:

  • "She looked askance at the contract, sensing something was hidden in the fine print."

→ She didn't accept it openly. She read it with suspicion and caution.

  • "The villagers looked askance at the newcomer who never greeted anyone."

→ The villagers were suspicious of and uneasy about the newcomer.

  • "He looked askance at his colleague's sudden friendliness, knowing they had argued just the day before."

→ He found the friendliness suspicious and didn't trust it.

  • "Many scientists looked askance at the study because its methods were poorly explained."

→ The scientific community viewed it with doubt and disapproval, not accepting it at face value.

  • "The bank manager looked askance at the loan application filled with vague answers."

→ He was doubtful and disapproving, not ready to accept it without question.

"Askance" is not a word of violent emotion. It does not mean anger, hatred, or outrage. The feeling it carries is quieter and more internal than that. It can hold any of the following, alone or in combination:

  • Suspicion — "Something is not right here."
  • Distrust — "I don't believe this is entirely honest."
  • Doubt or skepticism — "I'm not convinced this is true or good."
  • Mild disapproval — "I don't think much of this."
  • Wariness — "I need to be careful around this."

The common thread running through all of them is that you are not accepting something openly or at face value. There is a reservation in you. A guard is up.

Literally, "look askance at" can describe a real, physical sideways glance — eyes slightly narrowed, head not fully turned toward the subject.

Figuratively (and this is by far the more common and important use), it means an attitude of suspicion or disapproval — even in situations where no actual looking is happening. For example:

  • "Society has long looked askance at artists who break traditional rules."

Here, "society" is not physically turning its eyes. The sentence means that society has generally regarded such artists with suspicion and disapproval. This figurative use is everywhere in formal writing, journalism, and literature.
The Register: When and Where Is This Word Used?

"Askance" is a formal to semi-formal word. You will encounter it most in:

  • Literature and novels
  • News articles and journalism
  • Academic or professional writing
  • Formal speech

In casual everyday conversation, people would more naturally say "he was suspicious of it" or "she didn't trust it" instead of using "askance." But the word is not so rare or old-fashioned that it sounds strange — it is a perfectly alive, active word in modern written English.

To make sure the meaning is crystal clear, here is what it does not mean:

  • It does not mean angry or furious. It is quieter than that.
  • It does not mean completely ignoring something. You are still looking at it — just not openly.
  • It does not mean shocked or surprised. The emphasis is on distrust and disapproval, not surprise.
  • It does not mean envious or jealous. Those are entirely different feelings.

If you had to capture the whole word in one sentence, it would be this:

To look askance at something or someone is to regard them with a quiet, guarded sense of suspicion, doubt, or disapproval — not accepting them openly or at face value.

Every time you see "askance," that is the feeling at its heart.
